[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday 'type' means a kind or label (a 'whole number' is still just a number), so novices read int and double as tags on the same arithmetic. In Java the type fixes both the set of values and which operation runs: 7 / 2 on two ints is 3, while 7.0 / 2 is 3.5.
[1] misconception (M) -> AllDoublesToAvoidDivision: wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.
[2] misconception (M) -> AnyValueInAnyVariable: wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> AllDoublesToAvoidDivision: Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

[0] names_the_element (N): Data type: a category of data defined as a set of values together with the set of operations on those values (int, double, boolean, char, String...).
[1] states_the_rule (S): Java is strongly typed: every variable and expression has a type known at compile time, a variable always holds a value of its type, and the compiler rejects values or operations that do not fit (int x = 1.1; does not compile).

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): For each operator, the operand types are found first (after any automatic promotion), and then that type's version of the operator is applied. So in b*b - 4*c with int b and c, the whole expression is computed as int and only then promoted to double for Math.sqrt().
[1] output_prediction (OP): The result type follows from the operand types: int op int gives int (7 / 2 is 3), any double operand gives double (7 / 2.0 is 3.5), and + with a String operand gives a String ("7" + 2 is "72").
[2] one_step_execution (OS): A declaration fixes a variable's type for good. Each assignment changes only the value, never the type, and a value outside the type (a double into an int) is rejected at compile time unless it is cast.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The eight primitive types are Java's built-in data types. Each one fixes its own values and operators (boolean has && || !, int has + - * / %), so which operators are legal in an expression depends on which primitive type its operands have.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A data structure such as an array holds many values of one data type. The element type limits what can be stored in a[i] and which operations apply to it.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Choosing a type records what a value represents (int for counts, double for measurements, boolean for conditions, String for text), so the compiler can check that operations match that intent.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> AllDoublesToAvoidDivision: Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Think in data types whenever you declare a variable or read an expression. Use the built-in primitive types for single numbers, characters and truth values, String for text, and an array or another class when no single built-in type has the values and operations you need.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A value can be stored only in a variable whose type can hold it without loss; narrowing needs an explicit cast. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Assigning a double (or long) expression to an int variable, e.g. int x = 1.1; or int n = Math.round(x);: 'incompatible types: possible lossy conversion'.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An operator is defined only for certain types. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Applying an operator to a type that lacks it: "Hello" - 1, s < t on Strings, !5: 'bad operand types for binary operator'.

A data structure organizes many values of a data type; the array holds a sequence of values of one type.
Java has eight primitive data types (boolean, char, byte, short, int, long, float, double); each, like any data type, is a set of values and a set of operations on those values.
